a2z-354.description:
Given an undirected graph with V vertices (0..V-1) as an adjacency list, count its connected components — maximal sets of vertices mutually reachable by paths.

Flood fill: keep a visited array; for each unvisited vertex launch a DFS/BFS that marks its whole component and increment a counter once per launch. Isolated vertices count as components of size 1. O(V + E) time, O(V) space — the same skeleton as number-of-islands but on a general graph.

examples.explanation: Components {0,1,2} and {3,4}.
Every isolated vertex is its own component.

constraints: 0 <= E <= 10^5; graph undirected, no self-loops required
O(V + E) time; iterative DFS or explicit queue to avoid stack overflow

a2z-355.description:
Given a connected undirected graph with V vertices and its adjacency list, produce both traversal orders: DFS (deep-first, backtracking) and BFS (level-by-level), each printed as the sequence of first visits starting from vertex 0 (neighbors visited in adjacency-list order).

DFS: recurse (or use a stack) marking vertices visited on first touch, emitting before descending. BFS: seed a queue with 0, pop-then-push-unvisited-neighbours, emitting at enqueue time so order is by nondecreasing depth. Both run in O(V + E); the exercise contrasts the stack/queue that produce different orders on the same graph.

examples.explanation: DFS dives 0-1-3 and reaches 2 through 3; BFS takes 1 and 2 as direct neighbours of 0 first.
Single vertex.

constraints: Graph connected; undirected edges stored both ways
O(V + E); visit neighbours in listed order

a2z-356.description:
Given an undirected connected graph as an adjacency list and a starting vertex, print the depth-first search order — vertices in the order DFS first visits them.

Mark the start visited and emit it; recurse into each unvisited neighbour in list order. Iterative form: push the start on a stack, pop, and if unvisited emit + mark, then push neighbours in reverse list order so the smallest-listed neighbour pops first. O(V + E).

examples.explanation: From 0 go deep to 1, then 4, backtrack to 3 (via 4) or from 0's list after 1's subtree — order follows adjacency lists and visited marking.

examples.input: start vertex 2 in the same graph
examples.explanation: Same rule from a different seed.

constraints: O(V + E); each vertex printed exactly once

a2z-358.description:
Given an R × C grid of 0s (water) and 1s (land), count the connected components of land where cells connect in all 8 directions (horizontal, vertical and diagonal). A single island is any 8-connected group of 1-cells.

Classic flood fill: for each unvisited land cell run DFS/BFS over its 8-neighbour component, marking visited (or sinking the island by zeroing cells), incrementing the count per launch. O(R·C) time. The 8-directional move list is the one detail separating this from Number of Islands (4-directional).

examples.explanation: The diagonal touch at (0,0)-(1,1) and the cluster around (1,4),(2,3),(2,4) merge single-cell islands.
One land cell is one island.

constraints: O(R·C·8) time; iterative DFS or bounded recursion

a2z-361.description:
Detect whether an undirected graph (V vertices, adjacency list, possibly disconnected) contains a cycle, using BFS.

Component-wise BFS carrying each vertex's parent: when reaching an already-visited neighbour that is not the parent, a cycle exists (the two BFS paths to that neighbour close a loop). Multi-source loop over unvisited starts handles disconnected graphs. O(V + E). The DFS analogue flags a back edge to a visited non-parent; parallel-edge inputs make the parent-value check insufficient — a parent-edge check is the strict form.

examples.explanation: Triangle 0-1-2-0; BFS from 0 reaches 2 from 1 while 2 is already visited and not 1's parent.
Every revisited neighbour is the parent — trees never trigger the condition.

constraints: O(V + E) BFS with parent tracking

a2z-371.description:
Given a directed acyclic graph with V vertices and M edges, output a topological ordering — a linear arrangement in which every edge u→v places u before v. Solve with DFS: run DFS over the graph, push each vertex onto a list when it finishes (postorder), then reverse the list.

A finished vertex has all its successors already emitted, so reverse-postorder satisfies every edge. Any DAG can have many valid orders; any one is accepted. Visited marking makes each edge processed once: O(V + M). Running the same DFS on a graph with a cycle surfaces a back edge — the DFS method doubles as cycle detection.

examples.explanation: Postorder finishes 0/1 first; reversed order starts at the source 3.
A chain has one topological order.

constraints: 0 <= M <= 10^5; graph guaranteed acyclic for this variant
O(V + M); recursion depth may need an iterative DFS

a2z-372.description:
Topologically sort a directed graph with V vertices and M edges using Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees), and report whether a valid order exists (the graph may contain cycles).

Compute in-degree of every vertex; enqueue all with in-degree 0; repeatedly dequeue, append to the order, and decrement successors' in-degrees, enqueuing any that reach 0. If the order holds fewer than V vertices the remaining ones sit on cycles — report an empty order / cycle flag. Queue-pop order decides between multiple valid orders (a min-priority queue yields the lexicographically smallest). O(V + M).

examples.explanation: In-degrees: 0 for 4,5; 1 becomes last when 0 and 3 release it.
No in-degree-0 vertex; the queue starts empty.

constraints: 0 <= M <= 10^5; graph may be cyclic — detect it

a2z-378.description:
Given an undirected graph with unit-weight edges (adjacency list, V vertices) and a source vertex S, compute the shortest distance from S to every vertex; output -1 for unreachable vertices.

Plain BFS from S: the first time a vertex is dequeued, its BFS depth is the shortest path length, because BFS processes vertices in nondecreasing depth and every edge costs 1. Distances start at -1, dist[S] = 0. O(V + E) — Dijkstra is unnecessary overhead here, and DFS gives no shortest-path guarantee.

examples.explanation: 4 sits three hops away via 0-1-3-4 (or 0-2-3-4).
The second component is unreachable.

a2z-379.description:
Given a weighted directed acyclic graph with V vertices (0..V-1) and adjacency list entries (node, weight), find the shortest distances from a source node S to every vertex; print -1e9 (or Infinity/-1 per the platform) for unreachable vertices.

Two-step linear algorithm: (1) topologically sort the DAG; (2) relax every edge in topological order — dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w) while sweeping u from sources to sinks. Once a vertex is processed no later edge can improve it. O(V + E), and unlike Dijkstra it also handles negative weights; a cycle would invalidate the sweep, which is exactly why the DAG promise matters.

examples.explanation: Nothing to relax.

constraints: Weights can be negative; graph guaranteed acyclic
O(V + E); no priority queue needed

a2z-380.description:
Given a weighted, undirected, connected graph with non-negative edge weights as an adjacency list (V vertices, source 0), compute the shortest distance from the source to every vertex — Dijkstra's algorithm.

Maintain dist[] (∞ except dist[S]=0) and a min-priority queue keyed by distance: extract the closest settled vertex u, relax each edge (u,v,w) with dist[v] > dist[u]+w, pushing improved v. Lazy deletion (skip stale heap entries whose dist already improved) replaces decrease-key. Once popped with the current best distance, a vertex is final — non-negative weights mean no future path can beat it. O((V + E) log V).

examples.explanation: Path 0-2-1 (1+2) beats the direct edge 4; then +1 to 3.
Trivial.

constraints: O((V+E) log V); distances may need 64-bit

a2z-381.description:
Explain (and demonstrate on a trace) why Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority queue instead of a plain array scan or a FIFO queue: which operation must be fast, what the choice costs per vertex/edge, and what breaks without it.

The greedy step needs the *unvisited vertex with minimum tentative distance* — an array scan finds it in O(V), giving O(V²) total (fine for dense graphs); a min-heap (or std::set/priority_queue) extracts and inserts in O(log V) for O((V+E) log V), dominating on sparse graphs; an ordinary queue loses the ordering guarantee and can settle vertices prematurely. Without decrease-key support, push duplicates and skip stale pops — lazy deletion. The answer should also note the non-negative-weight precondition: Dijkstra itself, heap or not, fails on negative edges.

examples.output: heap version ~O(E log V) ≈ 1.7·10^6 ops vs array O(V²) = 10^10 — heap wins
examples.explanation: Extraction dominates and the heap avoids rescanning all distances.

examples.output: array scan O(V²) matches or beats heap O(E log V)
examples.explanation: log V overhead on V² edges tips it back to the simple implementation.

constraints: Conceptual exercise; include a worked graph trace where a FIFO queue settles a vertex too early
Cover: greedy min-extraction, lazy deletion vs decrease-key, complexity comparison
Mention why negative weights still break the greedy invariant

a2z-387.description:
Given a start value, a target (end) value, and an array of multipliers, transform start into end by repeatedly replacing the current value x with (x × a[i]) % 100000 for any i. Return the minimum number of multiplications needed, or -1 if end is unreachable. (Striver's 'Minimum Multiplications to reach End'.)

Every value 0..99999 is a node; each of the (≤9) multipliers defines an unweighted directed edge x → (x·a) mod 100000. Shortest path in an unweighted graph = BFS from start over the residue space, dist[] initialized to -1. Building the 10^5×9 edges explicitly is unnecessary — generate neighbours on the fly. O(100000 × k).

examples.explanation: 2×2 = 4 then 4×7 = 28 (or 2×7 = 14, 14×2 = 28); one multiplication is not enough ({4, 10, 14} excludes 28).
Every reachable residue is 9·2^k mod 100000 — the factor 9 can never vanish, so 2 is unreachable.

constraints: O(100000 × k) BFS over the residue graph

a2z-388.description:
Given a weighted directed graph with V vertices, M edges (u, v, w) where w may be negative, and source 0, find the shortest distances to all vertices; return {-1} if the graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable in a way that improves paths. (GFG Bellman-Ford formulation.)

Relax all M edges V-1 times: after i passes, every shortest path with ≤ i edges is finalized — a simple path uses at most V-1 edges, so V-1 rounds suffice whether or not negative edges exist. One extra pass: any edge that still relaxes proves a negative cycle. O(V·M) — slower than Dijkstra but strictly more expressive (negative edges), and it detects the cases where shortest paths are undefined.

examples.explanation: dist[2] = min(4, 5-2) = 3 by pass 2; dist[4] = 6; dist[3] = min(3+6, 6+2) = 8. Negative edge 1→2 handled fine.
Cycle 1→2→1 costs -5: pass V still relaxes edge 2→1, proving a negative cycle.

constraints: O(V·M); report [-1] on any negative cycle found in pass V

a2z-389.description:
Given a weighted directed graph as an adjacency matrix (adj[i][j] = weight, or -1 for 'no edge', zero diagonal), compute the shortest distance between every ordered pair of vertices — the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs DP.

dist[i][j] = min over all intermediate sets { paths using vertices 0..k as intermediates }, updated k-in-the-outer-loop: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). The k-major loop order is mandatory (it is the DP stage, not an interchangeable nesting). Initialize with edge weights and 0 diagonal; translate unreachable pairs to -1 on output (per GFG convention). O(V³) time, O(V²) space; detects negative cycles when dist[i][i] < 0 appears.

examples.explanation: Via vertex 1: 0→1→2 costs 1+7 = 8, beating the direct 43; vertex 2 has no outgoing edges so its row keeps -1s.
1→0→2 gives dist[1][2] = 2+3 = 5; the 2↔0 and 2→1 pairs stay unreachable.

constraints: O(V³) triple loop, k outermost; print 0 on diagonal

a2z-392.description:
Given a weighted, connected, undirected graph as an adjacency list (V vertices, E edges), compute the total weight of its Minimum Spanning Tree using Prim's algorithm.

Grow one tree from vertex 0: keep a min-heap of candidate edges crossing the cut; repeatedly pop the cheapest edge, and if it leads to an unvisited vertex, add its weight, mark that vertex, and push all its outgoing edges. Each vertex joins once → V-1 accepted edges. O((V + E) log V) with the heap (dense-graph O(V²) array variant scans min key). Correct by the cut property: the lightest edge across any cut is safe for the MST.

examples.explanation: Single forced edge.

constraints: O((V+E) log V); skip stale heap entries for visited vertices

a2z-393.description:
Implement a Disjoint Set Union (union-find) structure over n elements 0..n-1 supporting find(x) (which component?), union(x, y) (merge components) and component count/size queries — with path compression and union by rank (or size) so operations run in effectively constant amortized time.

Each component is a rooted tree: find walks parent[] up to the root; path compression re-points every visited node directly at the root. Union attaches the smaller-rank (or smaller-size) root under the larger — keeping trees shallow. α(n) inverse-Ackermann amortized bound. Application follow-ups: Kruskal MST, cycle detection in undirected graphs (union finds two endpoints already together), account-merge style grouping problems.

examples.input: union(0,1), union(2,3), union(1,2), find(3) then find(0)
examples.explanation: Second union merges the two pairs; ranks keep the tree depth ≤ 2.

examples.input: union(4,5), then query find(4) == find(5)? find(4) == find(0)?
examples.explanation: Two separate components remain.

constraints: Both find and union amortized O(α(n)); parent + rank/size arrays only

a2z-394.description:
Given a connected, weighted, undirected graph with V vertices and E edges (u, v, weight), return the total weight of its Minimum Spanning Tree — the acyclic edge subset connecting all vertices of minimum summed weight. Solve with Kruskal: sort edges by weight, then greedily accept an edge whenever its endpoints lie in different components (DSU), stopping at V-1 accepted edges.

Sorting dominates at O(E log E); each union/find is near O(1) via path compression + rank. Correct via the cut/cycle property: skipping an edge whose endpoints are already connected can never force a more expensive future choice. The Prim variant (heap over frontier edges, O((V+E) log V)) is the sibling solution.

examples.explanation: Cheapest two edges; the third closes a cycle.

constraints: O(E log E) with DSU; result fits in 64-bit

a2z-402.description:
Find all articulation points (cut vertices) of a connected undirected graph — vertices whose removal increases the number of connected components. (GFG articulation-point formulation; print them sorted.)

One DFS computing disc[u] (discovery time) and low[u] (earliest discovery reachable from u's subtree using ≤ one back edge). u is an articulation point if: (a) u is the DFS root with ≥ 2 DFS children, or (b) u is non-root and has a child v with low[v] >= disc[u] — v's subtree cannot reach above u. Mark each u once despite multiple triggering children. O(V + E). Bridges use the stricter test low[v] > disc[u].

examples.explanation: Removing 1 or 3 disconnects the graph; the triangle 0-1-2 shields its other vertices (low values fall below discovery times).
Every vertex stays connected after one removal; no articulation points.

constraints: 0 <= E <= 10^5; undirected connected (run DFS per component if not)
O(V + E) single DFS; skip only the direct parent edge once

a2z-460.description:
Implement a Trie (prefix tree) over lowercase English letters supporting: insert(word), search(word) → does the exact word exist?, startsWith(prefix) → is it a prefix of any stored word?, and the advanced operations — delete(word) and countWords(prefix).

Each node stores up to 26 child pointers and an endOfWord flag; insert walks/slots down one char per level; search must additionally check the terminal flag (a present path alone only proves prefixhood). Delete = walk down recording the last node with >1 child (or a terminal), then prune the unshared suffix. count(prefix) walks to the prefix node and sums terminals in its subtree — precompute a subtree word-count field per node to answer in O(|prefix|). Time is proportional to word length for every operation; space O(total inserted characters).

examples.explanation: 'app' is a path but not terminal.
Only the 'car' terminal flag clears — the 'cart' branch survives.

constraints: O(L) per operation; 26-way node array or map

a2z-463.description:
Bit prerequisites for binary-Trie problems: work fluently with the fixed-width binary view of integers that maximum-XOR / minimum-XOR trie queries rest on — extract bit i of x as (x >> i) & 1, read numbers MSB-first (bit 31 down to 0 for 32-bit ints), and use XOR identities: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and a set bit in the xor result means the operands differ at that position.

The exercises: print the 32-bit representation of given integers, compute pairwise XORs, and reason why a greedy MSB-first walk maximizes a XOR against a stored set (at each level prefer the opposite bit — it sets a higher-order 1 which dominates all lower bits combined). This warm-up makes the binary trie (max-XOR query) mechanical: bits are just the alphabet {0,1}.

examples.explanation: (5 >> i) & 1 for each i isolates bit i; for 32-bit ints run i = 31 down to 0.
5^1 = 4, 5^4 = 1, 5^7 = 2. Greedily the top differing bit wins: 5 = 101, preferring y with bit-2 = 0 (y = 1) sets the 4's place, which outweighs everything below.

constraints: Bit indices 30 down to 0 are enough for non-negative ints
No trie required yet — pure bit manipulation drills

a2z-470.description: Compute the Z-array of a string s of length n: Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of s (Z[0] is conventionally 0 or n). Use it for linear pattern search: build Z on pattern + '#' + text — any position with Z-value |pattern| is an occurrence.

examples.explanation: i=1: "aabaab" shares "aa" with the prefix, breaks at b vs a; i=4: "aab" shares "aa"; single letters elsewhere.
i=2: "abcab" matches prefix "ab" then c ≠ a; i=5: "ab" matches to the end of string.

constraints: Lowercase alphabet; separator '#' must not appear in pattern/text

a2z-471.description:
Implement KMP: precompute the LPS (longest proper prefix which is also suffix) array for a pattern, then search a text in linear time, never backtracking the text pointer.

LPS construction: lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pat[0..i] equal to its suffix, built by falling back j = lps[j-1] on mismatches. Search mirrors it: on mismatch between text[i] and pattern[j], retry with j = lps[j-1] (a matched border stays matched); emit a hit whenever j reaches |pattern| and continue with j = lps[j-1] to allow overlaps. O(n + m); the naive O(n·m) scan is what the automaton view eliminates.

examples.explanation: LPS = [0,0,1,2,0,1,2,3,4]; after matching ABAB at text[10..13] a mismatch-free run completes the pattern at 18 — fallbacks at earlier D/C mismatches reuse the ABAB border instead of rewinding the text pointer.
Overlapping hits: after a match j resets to lps[1] = 1.

constraints: O(n + m) time, O(m) extra for LPS
